issues.legal_issue: Compensation for cancellation of a contract made in the ordinary course of business is a revenue receipt, even when the contract was to operate over a long period.
material_facts: The taxpayer carried on a business producing and supplying limestone and had entered into the contract as part of that business.
The parties cancelled the contract by agreement after the contemplated railway facilities were not provided, and the company paid compensation for the cancellation.
The taxpayer continued to obtain contracts for supplying limestone and loading iron ore, and was not prevented from carrying on business.
The compensation was not shown to reimburse capital expenditure thrown away in performing the contract.
issues.conclusion: The compensation was a revenue receipt chargeable to tax; the contract’s long duration did not make the receipt capital.
issues.legal_principle: The character of a receipt depends on the nature of the transaction and the business asset involved. Compensation for cancellation of an ordinary trading contract is generally a trading receipt, whether performance involved one act or a series of acts over time. A trading contract is part of the business itself, unlike an agency agreement that may be a capital asset or framework for business. The Court applied the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, and relied on Short Bros. Ltd. v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, Commissioners of Inland Revenue v. Northfleet Coal and Ballast Co. Ltd., Jessee Robinson & Sons v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, and Commissioner of Income-tax v. South India Pictures Ltd.; it distinguished Income-tax Commissioner v. Shaw Wallace & Co., Barr, Crombie & Co. Ltd. v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue, and Van Den Berghs Ltd. v. Clark. It also noted that compensation for a separate covenant not to compete or for capital expenditure thrown away may have a different character, and distinguished compensation for restraint imposed by an external authority, as in The Glenboig Union Fireclay Co. Ltd. v. Commissioners of Inland Revenue.

rule.if: income_tax_appeal and compensation_paid_for_contract_cancellation and contract_made_in_ordinary_business and not payment_for_abandoned_capital_expenditure and not payment_for_post_contract_noncompetition and not business_restrained_by_external_authority

predicates.income_tax_appeal: The proceeding concerns whether a receipt in a business context is taxable as income.
predicates.compensation_paid_for_contract_cancellat: One contracting party paid the other compensation in return for cancelling their contract.
predicates.contract_made_in_ordinary_business: The taxpayer entered into the contract as part of the ordinary conduct of its business.
predicates.payment_for_abandoned_capital_expenditur: The payment reimbursed capital expenditure that the taxpayer had incurred in performing the contract and then lost when it was cancelled.
predicates.payment_for_post_contract_noncompetition: The payment compensated the taxpayer for agreeing not to carry on similar business after the contract ended.
predicates.business_restrained_by_external_authorit: An external authority used an overriding power to prevent the taxpayer from carrying on its business.

issues.definition: When a taxable-income appeal concerns compensation for cancellation of an ordinary business contract, and the payment is not for abandoned capital expenditure or a post-contract restraint and the business was not restrained by an external authority, the compensation is treated as a taxable revenue receipt.

issues.legal_issue: A taxpayer’s claim that cancellation compensation reimbursed capital expenditure cannot establish capital treatment without evidence that the expenditure was incurred and that the compensation was paid for it.
material_facts: The taxpayer argued that the compensation reimbursed substantial expenditure on works connected with an earlier quarry arrangement.
The taxpayer did not establish that the claimed capital expenses had been incurred or that the compensation related to them.
The quarry associated with the earlier arrangement had been abandoned before the contract whose cancellation generated the compensation was made.
issues.conclusion: The compensation could not be treated as a capital receipt on the basis of reimbursement for capital expenditure.
issues.legal_principle: The character of a receipt must be determined on the facts established; a claimed connection to capital expenditure does not alter the receipt’s character without evidence supporting that connection. The Court applied the principles governing the distinction between capital and revenue receipts under the Indian Income-tax Act, 1922, including the approach described in Van Den Berghs Ltd. v. Clark.

predicates.income_tax_appeal: The proceeding concerns whether a receipt in a business context is taxable as income.
predicates.taxpayer_claims_capital_cost_reimburseme: The taxpayer asserts that compensation paid on cancellation reimbursed capital expenditure incurred in performing an arrangement.
predicates.no_evidence_supports_cost_or_connection: The taxpayer provides no evidence establishing the claimed expenditure or connecting it to the compensation.

issues.definition: If a taxpayer in a taxable-income appeal claims that cancellation compensation reimbursed capital costs but provides no evidence of the costs or their connection to the payment, that claim is rejected.
